title: Error and Harm in Healthcare
path: Quality Improvement in Healthcare and Patient Safety

headings.title: Introduction to Patient Safety and Healthcare Quality
headings.content: Patient safety remains the bedrock of professional nursing practice across Nigeria and the global community. Healthcare quality encompasses safety, effectiveness, patient-centeredness, timeliness, efficiency, and equity. When a patient walks into a clinic, tertiary hospital, or primary healthcare centre, they place ultimate trust in the multidisciplinary team. Safety is not merely the absence of accidents; it is the active creation of systems that make doing the right thing easier and doing the wrong thing harder. Nurses spend the most direct time at the bedside, positioning them as the final barrier against system failures that threaten client well-being.

headings.title: Defining Medical Error, Near Misses, and Adverse Events
headings.content:
- **Medical Error**: An unintended act of omission or commission during healthcare management that leads to, or has the potential to lead to, an undesirable outcome.
- **Near Miss**: An unplanned event that did not result in clinical harm, only because intercepted in time or by sheer luck.
- **Adverse Event**: An injury resulting from medical management rather than the underlying disease condition of the patient.

headings.title: Understanding Patient Harm and Its Classifications
headings.content:
Patient harm involves impairment of physical, emotional, or psychological structure or function of the body. In clinical settings, harm is categorized by severity to guide intervention and quality improvement.

| Severity Level | Clinical Description | Nursing Action Required |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mild | Symptoms are minimal, intervention is short-term | Monitor and document |
| Moderate | Requires intervention, prolongs hospital stay | Treat symptoms and notify physician |
| Severe | Life-threatening, causes permanent disability | Emergency response and resuscitation |
| Death | Patient demises as a direct result of the event | Post-mortem protocol and incident reporting |

headings.title: The Swiss Cheese Model: How and Why Errors Occur
headings.content: James Reason's Swiss Cheese Model explains that complex system failures rarely happen because of a single careless action. Instead, defenses in an organization are likened to slices of Swiss cheese aligned next to each other. Each slice represents a safety barrier, such as policy guidelines, double-checking medication, or proper equipment maintenance. The holes in the cheese represent weaknesses or active failures in those defenses. An error only causes harm when the holes in multiple slices temporarily align, allowing a hazard to pass straight through all defenses from start to finish.

headings.title: Common Types of Healthcare Errors in Clinical Practice
headings.content: Clinical errors manifest in several distinct categories during daily hospital routines. Medication administration errors remain frequent, involving wrong doses, incorrect timing, or omitted drugs. Diagnostic errors involve missed or delayed disease identification, often seen in busy outpatient clinics. Surgical mishaps include wrong-site surgery or retained foreign objects like swabs. Healthcare-associated infections represent another massive category of harm, driven by poor aseptic technique or inadequate hand hygiene compliance among ward personnel.

headings.title: The Impact of Healthcare Errors on Patients and Nursing Staff
headings.content: When errors occur, the toll extends far beyond physical injury. Patients suffer prolonged admissions, additional surgical procedures, permanent disability, or death, accompanied by a severe loss of trust in the healthcare system. Families bear emotional and financial burdens. Meanwhile, nurses involved in adverse events often experience 'second victim' syndrome. This psychological state involves profound guilt, anxiety, depression, burnout, and fear of litigation, which can compromise future clinical performance if institutional support is lacking.

headings.title: Root Cause Analysis and Reporting Culture in Nursing
headings.content: Root Cause Analysis (RCA) is a structured method used to identify the fundamental reasons for an adverse event or serious near miss. Instead of asking who made the mistake, RCA asks why the system allowed the mistake to happen. In many clinical environments, fear of punishment creates a culture of silence where errors go unreported. Establishing a robust reporting culture requires management to shift focus away from personal blame and toward system evaluation. Nurses must feel safe documenting and discussing errors openly to prevent future occurrences.

headings.title: Strategies for Error Prevention and Promoting a Just Culture
headings.content: Promoting safety requires deliberate, proactive strategies across all healthcare tiers. A 'Just Culture' recognizes that humans make mistakes and distinguishes between human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior. While reckless behavior is addressed, human errors and at-risk behaviors are used as learning opportunities to redesign systems. Practical bedside interventions include standardizing handoff communication using tools like SBAR, utilizing barcode medication administration, conducting safety briefings at shift changes, and encouraging patients to actively participate in their own care plans.
